angle: how credit card companies make money: numbers, psychology, playbook
title: How Credit Card Companies Make Money From You

scenes.text: Hi, I'm Ryan Rover. Here's a question most people never ask. Your credit card gives you rewards, a free app, fraud protection, sometimes even airport lounges. So who's paying for all of that? Because the card company isn't a charity. Today, we follow the money, and we find out exactly how credit card companies make money from you.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: In twenty twenty two, according to the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, credit card companies charged Americans more than one hundred billion dollars in interest, plus around twenty five billion dollars in fees.
scenes.short_hook: Who really pays for your credit card rewards?

scenes.text: That's not a typo. More than one hundred billion dollars in a single year, just in interest. And that's before we count the money merchants pay every time you swipe. Credit cards are one of the most profitable products in banking. Once you understand how that profit is made, you can use cards for their benefits while paying almost nothing.
scenes.caption: ONE OF BANKING'S BEST BUSINESSES

scenes.text: We'll look at it from three angles. First, the numbers: the eight main ways card companies earn money, and how much each one costs you. Second, the psychology: the design tricks that make you spend more and pay longer. And third, the playbook: how to flip the deal so the card works for you, not the other way around.
scenes.caption: FOLLOW THE MONEY

scenes.text: By the end, you'll know whether your card is a tool or a trap. Let's start with the money.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: Every number in this video comes from a named source. Interest and fee totals come from the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau's reports on the credit card market. Interest rates come from the Federal Reserve. Research on card payments comes from the Federal Reserve Bank of Boston. Where I show an example, it's stated, simple math. Card terms vary, so always read your own agreement. This is education, not financial advice.
scenes.caption: OUR SOURCES

scenes.text: Before the numbers, a quick story. Because to understand why cards work the way they do, it helps to know how they started.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: In nineteen fifty, a company called Diners Club launched a card that let members pay at a group of restaurants in New York and settle up later. It was a charge card. You paid the full bill each month. The business made money mainly from the restaurants, which paid a fee on every meal. That idea, that the merchant pays to accept the card, is still at the center of the system today.
scenes.caption: 1950: DINERS CLUB

scenes.text: In the late nineteen fifties, Bank of America took the idea further. In Fresno, California, it mailed tens of thousands of unsolicited credit cards to residents, a famous experiment known as the Fresno drop. These cards let people carry a balance and pay over time, with interest. Losses from fraud and unpaid balances were large at first, but the model eventually became BankAmericard, which later became Visa.
scenes.caption: THE FRESNO DROP

scenes.text: Then came a turning point. In nineteen seventy eight, a Supreme Court decision known as the Marquette case allowed national banks to charge the interest rate allowed in their home state to customers nationwide. Some states soon loosened their interest rate limits to attract card businesses. That's a big part of why so many card companies are based in states like South Dakota and Delaware, and why card rates can be so high.
scenes.caption: 1978: THE MARQUETTE CASE

scenes.text: Fast forward to two thousand nine. After the financial crisis, Congress passed the Credit CARD Act. It limited surprise rate increases on existing balances, required clearer statements, including the minimum payment warning, and restricted certain fees. It made cards fairer. But it didn't change the core business. Interest from people who carry balances, and fees from merchants on every swipe.
scenes.caption: 2009: THE CARD ACT

scenes.text: Angle one. The eight main ways card companies make money. Some you know. A few you probably don't.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: Way number one. Interest. By far the biggest money maker.
scenes.caption: WAY 1

scenes.text: When you don't pay your full statement balance by the due date, the card charges interest on what's left. According to the Federal Reserve, the average rate on card accounts that were charged interest has been above twenty percent in recent years. That's higher than almost any other common type of consumer loan.
scenes.caption: 20%+ A YEAR

scenes.text: Here's what that means. Carry a three thousand dollar balance all year at twenty two percent, and you pay roughly six hundred sixty dollars in interest. That's six hundred sixty dollars that buys nothing. Inside the industry, people who carry a balance are often called revolvers. They're the most profitable customers a card company has.
scenes.caption: ~$660 FOR NOTHING

scenes.text: There's a quiet detail most people miss. Card interest usually compounds daily. The card takes your yearly rate, divides it by three hundred sixty five, and applies it to your balance each day. Interest gets added to the balance, and tomorrow's interest is charged on that bigger number. It's the same compounding that grows investments, but working against you. Try this: find the APR on your statement right now. If you don't know it, that's the first problem.
scenes.caption: COMPOUNDED DAILY

scenes.text: Way number two. Swipe fees, also called interchange fees.

card.title: Swipe fees
card.sub: the merchant pays, then you do

scenes.caption: WAY 2

scenes.text: Every time you pay with a card, the store pays a fee, often somewhere around two percent of the purchase, sometimes more for premium rewards cards. Part goes to the bank that issued your card, part to the network and the processor. Across the whole country, merchants pay well over one hundred billion dollars a year in card processing fees.
scenes.caption: ~2% PER SWIPE

scenes.text: You might think, great, the store pays, not me. But stores build those costs into their prices. That means everyone pays a little more, including people who pay with cash or debit. Researchers at the Federal Reserve Bank of Boston studied this and found that, on average, cash users end up subsidizing card users, especially those with rewards cards.
scenes.caption: EVERYONE PAYS A LITTLE

scenes.text: This is how rewards are funded. That two percent cash back isn't free money from the bank. It's largely recycled from swipe fees, which come from higher prices for everyone. If you pay in full, you can come out ahead. If you carry a balance, the interest you pay can wipe out every reward many times over. Try this: compare your rewards earned this year with the interest you paid. Be honest about which is bigger.
scenes.caption: WHERE REWARDS COME FROM

scenes.text: Way number three. Late fees.
scenes.caption: WAY 3

scenes.text: Miss a due date, even by a day, and many cards charge a late fee that can be around thirty dollars or more. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau estimated that card companies charged roughly fourteen billion dollars in late fees in twenty twenty two alone. That's a lot of forgotten due dates.
scenes.caption: ~$14 BILLION IN LATE FEES

scenes.text: Late fees often don't come alone. A late payment can trigger a higher penalty interest rate, cancel a promotional rate, and, if it's thirty days late or more, show up on your credit report. One forgotten payment can cost the fee, months of higher interest and a lower score.
scenes.caption: ONE MISS, MANY COSTS

scenes.text: Card companies don't need you to be irresponsible. They just need you to be human. Busy weeks, a changed due date, a payment that didn't go through. The easiest defense is automation. Try this: set autopay for at least the minimum on every card, so you're never late, then pay the rest manually or set autopay to the full balance.
scenes.caption: NEVER BE LATE

scenes.text: Way number four. Annual fees.
scenes.caption: WAY 4

scenes.text: Many basic cards have no annual fee. But premium travel and rewards cards can charge from under one hundred dollars to several hundred dollars a year. In exchange, they offer bigger rewards, travel credits and perks. For the card company, the annual fee is steady, predictable income, paid whether you use the card or not.
scenes.caption: PAYING TO PAY

scenes.text: The perks are real, but only if you actually use them. A five hundred dollar card with a three hundred dollar travel credit is only worth it if you'd have spent that three hundred on travel anyway, and the rest of the perks matter to you. Many people pay for benefits they forget to claim.
scenes.caption: PERKS YOU USE

scenes.text: Card companies count on something called breakage, benefits that people are entitled to but never use. Unused credits, expired points, lounge passes that sit in an app. Every unused perk is profit. Try this: list every benefit of your fee card and what you actually used last year. If the total is less than the fee, ask for a no fee version, or a retention offer, before your renewal date.
scenes.caption: BREAKAGE

scenes.text: Way number five. Balance transfer fees.
scenes.caption: WAY 5

scenes.text: Balance transfer offers sound like a gift. Move your debt to a new card at zero percent interest for a year or more. But most charge a fee, commonly around three to five percent of the amount you move. Move ten thousand dollars at a three percent fee, and you pay three hundred dollars up front.
scenes.caption: 3-5% UP FRONT

scenes.text: That can still be a great deal compared with paying twenty two percent interest. The trap is what happens next. If the balance isn't paid off when the promotion ends, the regular rate kicks in. And many people, relieved by the zero percent, keep using the old card too. Now they have two balances.
scenes.query: Two credit cards side by side
scenes.caption: NOW TWO BALANCES

scenes.text: Card companies know a share of people won't finish in time. That's part of why the offers exist. Used with a plan, a balance transfer can save you a lot. Used as relief, it just delays the problem. Try this: before transferring, divide the balance by the number of promotional months. If you can't pay that amount every month, the offer probably won't solve your problem.
scenes.caption: DIVIDE BY THE MONTHS

scenes.text: Way number six. Cash advances.
scenes.caption: WAY 6

scenes.text: Using your credit card to get cash from an ATM is called a cash advance, and it's usually one of the most expensive ways to borrow. There's often an upfront fee, commonly around five percent or a minimum dollar amount. The interest rate is often higher than your purchase rate. And there's usually no grace period, so interest starts the day you take the cash.
scenes.caption: THE MOST EXPENSIVE CASH

scenes.text: Take five hundred dollars in a cash advance, and you might pay a twenty five dollar fee right away, plus interest at a higher rate from day one. Some things also count as cash advances without looking like one, like some money transfers, buying certain gambling chips, or some purchases that are treated like cash. Check your card's terms.
scenes.caption: HIDDEN CASH ADVANCES

scenes.text: People usually take cash advances when they're already stressed, which is why they're so profitable. The real fix is upstream: a small emergency fund so you never need one. Try this: ask your bank to lower or turn off the cash advance limit on your card. It removes the option on your worst day.
scenes.caption: TURN IT OFF

scenes.text: Way number seven. Foreign transaction fees.
scenes.caption: WAY 7

scenes.text: Many cards charge a fee, often around three percent, on purchases made in another currency or processed by a foreign bank. That includes buying something online from an overseas store, even if you never leave home. Spend two thousand dollars on a trip abroad, and that's about sixty dollars in fees.
scenes.caption: ~3% ON FOREIGN PURCHASES

scenes.text: There's a related trap at the register abroad. Sometimes the card machine asks if you want to pay in dollars instead of the local currency. It sounds convenient. But that conversion, called dynamic currency conversion, often uses a worse exchange rate set by the merchant's processor.
scenes.caption: PAY IN LOCAL CURRENCY

scenes.text: Many cards, especially travel cards, don't charge foreign transaction fees at all. So this one is easy to avoid if you check before you go. Try this: before your next trip or international online order, look up your card's foreign fee. And at foreign terminals, generally choose to pay in the local currency.
scenes.caption: CHECK BEFORE YOU GO

scenes.text: Way number eight. Penalty APRs.
scenes.caption: WAY 8

scenes.text: Many cards have a penalty rate, a much higher interest rate that can apply after you pay late, often if you're sixty days or more behind. Penalty rates on some cards approach thirty percent. Federal rules under the Credit CARD Act of two thousand nine limit when and how these can be applied, and require the issuer to review it later, but it can still be very expensive while it lasts.
scenes.caption: UP TO ~30%

scenes.text: Picture a five thousand dollar balance moving from twenty two percent to nearly thirty percent. That's roughly four hundred dollars more in interest per year, on top of late fees. It's the card company's way of charging more to customers it now considers riskier. And riskier customers who keep paying are very profitable.
scenes.caption: CALL BEFORE YOU'RE LATE

scenes.text: The good news: penalty rates are entirely avoidable. Pay at least the minimum, on time, every month. If you're struggling, call the issuer before you miss a payment. Many have hardship programs that can lower your rate or payment temporarily. Try this: save your card issuer's phone number in your contacts, under call before I'm late.
scenes.caption: SAVE THE NUMBER

scenes.text: So that's the money side. Interest, swipe fees, late fees, annual fees, balance transfer fees, cash advances, foreign fees and penalty rates. Notice something. Almost every one of them is avoidable. People who pay in full, on time, at home, pay close to nothing, and still collect rewards. People who carry a balance and slip up now and then fund the whole system.
scenes.caption: WHO FUNDS THE SYSTEM

scenes.text: Here's the contrast in a single picture. A cardholder who pays in full can earn rewards and pay no interest. A cardholder who carries three thousand dollars at twenty two percent pays roughly six hundred sixty dollars a year.

card.note: Illustration. Your card's terms will differ.

scenes.text: Now the part the card companies really don't advertise. How the product is designed to change your behavior.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: Angle two. The psychology. Five design tricks that keep you spending more and paying longer.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: Way number nine. The minimum payment anchor.
scenes.caption: WAY 9
scenes.short_hook: The minimum payment is designed to keep you in debt

scenes.text: Your statement shows several numbers: the full balance, and a much smaller minimum payment. Research by psychologist Neil Stewart found that showing the minimum payment can act as an anchor, a number your brain latches onto. In his experiments, people who saw a minimum payment tended to choose to repay less than people who didn't see one.
scenes.caption: THE ANCHOR

scenes.text: The minimum is often calculated as a small percent of the balance plus interest. It's designed to keep your account in good standing, not to get you out of debt. At the minimum, a balance of a few thousand dollars can take many years to clear, and the total interest can approach or even exceed what you originally spent.
scenes.caption: YEARS AT THE MINIMUM

scenes.text: Since the Credit CARD Act, statements must show how long it would take to pay off your balance making only minimum payments, and how much you'd pay in total. Most people skip that box. Try this: find it on your next statement and read it out loud. Then choose a fixed monthly payment that clears the balance in the time you want, and set it as your autopay.
scenes.caption: READ THE BOX

scenes.text: Way number ten. Rewards that change how you spend.
scenes.caption: WAY 10

scenes.text: Points, miles and cash back feel like free money. And that feeling changes behavior. People may choose a card purchase over cash to earn points, spend a bit more to hit a bonus, or book a hotel they didn't need to keep a status level. The reward is small. The extra spending can be large.
scenes.caption: POINTS FEEL FREE

scenes.text: Sign up bonuses are the clearest example. Spend four thousand dollars in three months, get a big bonus. If you were going to spend that anyway, great. If the bonus makes you buy things to reach the target, the card company just turned a reward into new spending, and possibly new interest.
scenes.caption: SPENDING FOR THE BONUS

scenes.text: Rewards also use gamification. Progress bars, status tiers, limited time offers, all designed to keep you engaged. Try this: treat rewards as a discount on spending you already planned, never as a reason to spend. And if you ever carry a balance, forget rewards completely and focus on the interest rate.
scenes.caption: GAMIFIED SPENDING

scenes.text: Way number eleven. Deferred interest promotions.
scenes.caption: WAY 11

scenes.text: You've seen it at furniture and electronics stores. No interest if paid in full in twelve months. That wording matters. With many of these store card offers, if you don't pay the entire balance by the deadline, interest is charged back to the original purchase date, on the full amount, not just what's left.
scenes.caption: IF PAID IN FULL

scenes.text: Say you buy a two thousand dollar couch on a twelve month deferred interest plan at twenty six percent, and you've paid it down to two hundred dollars when the year ends. On many of these plans, you could be charged roughly a year of interest on the full two thousand, potentially hundreds of dollars, all at once. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau has warned consumers about exactly this.
scenes.caption: INTEREST FROM DAY ONE

scenes.text: This is different from a true zero percent APR card, where interest only starts on the remaining balance after the promotion. The words if paid in full are the warning sign. Try this: if you use a deferred interest offer, divide the price by the months, minus one, and pay that amount every month so you finish early.
scenes.caption: READ THE WORDS

scenes.text: Way number twelve. Automatic credit limit increases.
scenes.caption: WAY 12

scenes.text: Card companies often raise your limit over time, sometimes without you asking. It feels like a compliment. You've been trusted with more. And a higher limit can actually help your score, by lowering how much of your available credit you're using.
scenes.caption: MORE ROOM

scenes.text: But for some people, a higher limit simply becomes more room to spend. Research on consumer behavior has suggested that people often treat available credit as part of what they can afford. If you were already carrying a balance, a higher limit can mean a higher balance, and more interest.
scenes.caption: AVAILABLE CREDIT ISN'T INCOME

scenes.text: The key is knowing which type of person you are. If you pay in full every month, a higher limit is mostly a benefit. If you carry a balance, it's a risk. Try this: if limit increases tempt you, call and ask to keep your limit where it is, or set your own spending alert well below it.
scenes.caption: SET YOUR OWN LIMIT

scenes.text: Way number thirteen. Making payment painless.
scenes.caption: WAY 13

scenes.text: Paying with cash makes you feel the money leave. Researchers call that the pain of paying. Cards reduce that pain, and studies have suggested people may spend more when paying by card. Tap to pay, phone wallets and one click checkouts reduce it even further. Less pain, more spending.
scenes.caption: NO PAIN, MORE SPENDING

scenes.text: Card companies and retailers work hard to remove friction. Saved cards in every app. Approval in a second. No signature. Each step makes buying easier, which is great for convenience, and great for spending. Convenience is the product, and your spending is the result.
scenes.caption: FRICTION REMOVED

scenes.text: You don't have to give up convenience. You just need to add one deliberate pause. Try this: remove saved cards from shopping sites and apps you use for impulse buys. Keep them only for bills and essentials. That small pause is often enough to ask, do I actually want this?
scenes.caption: ADD ONE PAUSE

scenes.text: Here's something worth knowing. Card companies think about you as a journey, from the first offer to the last payment. Let me walk you through it.
scenes.caption: RYAN
scenes.chapter: The customer journey they plan for

scenes.text: It starts with acquisition. Mail offers, app pop ups, and sign up bonuses at checkout. Card companies spend heavily to win new customers, because a good customer can be profitable for many years. That's why so many offers arrive in your mailbox, and why the bonus is so big. They expect to earn it back.
scenes.caption: STAGE 1: THE OFFER

scenes.text: Next comes activation and habit. The goal is to make the card your default. Put it in your phone wallet. Save it in your favorite apps. Earn extra points in your most common category. Once a card is the one you reach for without thinking, it tends to stay there for years.
scenes.caption: STAGE 2: THE HABIT

scenes.text: Then the profitable stage. If you carry a balance, interest flows every month. If you pay in full, swipe fees still flow. Limit increases, balance transfer offers and new promotions keep you engaged. And finally, retention. If you call to cancel, many issuers will offer bonus points, a waived fee or a lower rate to keep you. Which tells you something useful. Your business is worth more to them than you think.
scenes.caption: STAGES 3 AND 4: PROFIT AND RETENTION

scenes.text: Knowing this journey gives you leverage. You can take the sign up bonus on spending you'd do anyway. You can choose which card becomes your default. You can call before your annual fee posts and ask for a retention offer. And you can walk away if the deal stops working for you. You're the customer. Act like one.
scenes.caption: USE YOUR LEVERAGE

scenes.text: Quick pause. If you just realized your card has been making money off you, subscribe to the channel. It's free, and it helps me make more videos like this one. Now, let's flip the deal.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: Angle three. The playbook. Ten rules that make your card company earn almost nothing from you, while you keep the benefits.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: Rule one. Pay the full statement balance every month. This single habit removes the biggest source of card profit, interest. Most cards give you a grace period, so if you pay the full statement balance by the due date, new purchases don't get charged interest at all.
scenes.caption: RULE 1: PAY IN FULL
scenes.short_hook: 10 rules so your credit card makes $0 from you

scenes.text: Rule two. Turn on autopay. At least the minimum, ideally the full balance. You'll never pay a late fee or trigger a penalty rate again. Rule three. Know your APR. Write it down. If you ever carry a balance, that's the number that matters, not the rewards.
scenes.caption: RULES 2 AND 3

scenes.text: Rule four. If you carry a balance, attack it before anything else except a small emergency fund. Paying off a card at twenty two percent is a guaranteed twenty two percent return. Few investments can match that reliably. Rule five. Use balance transfers only with a written plan to finish before the promotion ends.
scenes.caption: RULES 4 AND 5

scenes.text: Here's why rule four matters. A three thousand dollar balance at twenty two percent. Paying only around the minimum can take many years. Paying a fixed three hundred dollars a month clears it in about twelve months.

Rule six. Never take a cash advance. Ask your issuer to lower or remove the cash limit if you can. Rule seven. Avoid deferred interest offers unless you'll pay them off early, with a fixed monthly amount set from day one.
scenes.caption: RULES 6 AND 7

scenes.text: Rule eight. Match the card to your life. If you don't travel, you may not need a travel card with an annual fee. If you travel abroad, pick a card with no foreign transaction fee. A simple no fee card with flat cash back is the right answer for many people.
scenes.caption: RULE 8: MATCH YOUR LIFE

scenes.text: Rule nine. Treat rewards as a discount, not a goal. Never spend to earn points. And once a year, add up what you earned and what you paid in fees and interest. If the second number is bigger, the card is winning. Rule ten. Read your statement every month. It takes five minutes, catches fraud and errors, and keeps you out of the ostrich effect.
scenes.caption: RULES 9 AND 10

scenes.text: Do these ten things, and you become what the industry sometimes calls a transactor. Someone who uses the card for convenience and pays in full. You still get the protection and rewards. And the card company earns mostly from the swipe fees, not from you directly.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: Now, let's read a credit card statement the way the card company does. Five numbers matter.
scenes.caption: RYAN
scenes.chapter: Reading your statement like an insider

scenes.text: Number one, the statement balance. That's what you owe for the last billing cycle. Pay this full amount by the due date, and on most cards you won't pay interest on purchases. Number two, the current balance. That includes new purchases made after the statement closed. You don't have to pay those yet to avoid interest, but you can.
scenes.caption: STATEMENT VS CURRENT

scenes.text: Number three, the minimum payment. As we saw, this is the anchor. Paying only this keeps your account in good standing, but keeps the interest flowing. Number four, the due date. Miss it, and fees and possibly a penalty rate follow. Number five, the APR. Often there are several: one for purchases, one for balance transfers, one for cash advances, and a penalty rate.
scenes.caption: MINIMUM, DUE DATE, APR

scenes.text: And then there's the box most people skip, the minimum payment warning. It shows how long it would take to pay off your balance with minimum payments only, and the total cost. It also shows what you'd need to pay each month to clear it in three years. That second number is often a much better target than the minimum. Try this: use the three year number as your new minimum.
scenes.caption: THE THREE YEAR NUMBER

scenes.text: One more line worth checking every month is the interest charged. If that line shows anything other than zero, you're paying for the privilege of borrowing. Seeing that number in black and white, month after month, is often what finally pushes people to change. Circle it. Write it on a sticky note. Make it visible until it reaches zero.
scenes.caption: CIRCLE THE INTEREST LINE

scenes.text: Let's make it real with two people holding the exact same rewards card, with two percent cash back and a twenty two percent APR. Alex spends about two thousand dollars a month on the card, and pays it off completely every month on autopay.
scenes.query: Young man with phone and card
scenes.caption: ALEX: THE TRANSACTOR
scenes.short_hook: Same credit card, two very different results

scenes.text: Over a year, Alex earns roughly four hundred eighty dollars in cash back. He pays no interest, no late fees, and no annual fee. The card company still makes money from Alex, through swipe fees paid by merchants, but Alex comes out ahead. For him, the card is a tool.
scenes.caption: +$480 A YEAR

scenes.text: Now Jordan. Same card, same spending. But Jordan pays only part of each bill, and carries an average balance of around six thousand dollars. Twice a year, Jordan forgets a payment and gets a late fee.
scenes.query: Woman stressed with bills at desk
scenes.caption: JORDAN: THE REVOLVER

scenes.text: Jordan also earns around four hundred eighty dollars in cash back. But on a six thousand dollar average balance at twenty two percent, Jordan pays roughly thirteen hundred dollars a year in interest, plus about sixty dollars in late fees. Net result, Jordan loses roughly nine hundred dollars a year. Same card. Same rewards. Opposite outcomes.
scenes.caption: -$900 A YEAR

scenes.text: Same card, same spending, same rewards. The only difference is paying in full.

card.note: Illustration at 22% APR and 2% cash back.

scenes.text: And here's the twist. Jordan's interest helps pay for the system that funds Alex's rewards. That's the quiet truth of credit cards. The people who pay in full are, in a way, subsidized by the people who don't. The goal of this video is to move you from Jordan's side to Alex's.
scenes.caption: WHO SUBSIDIZES WHOM

scenes.text: Let's do the honest math on premium cards, because they're everywhere. Imagine a card with a five hundred fifty dollar annual fee. It offers a three hundred dollar travel credit, airport lounge access, and three points per dollar on travel and dining. Is it worth it? It depends entirely on how you live.
scenes.caption: THE $550 QUESTION
scenes.chapter: When a fancy card is worth it

scenes.text: If you travel several times a year, use the full travel credit on trips you'd take anyway, and value the lounge, the math can work. Say you spend ten thousand dollars a year on travel and dining. At three points per dollar, that's thirty thousand points. Depending on how you redeem them, that might be worth around three hundred to four hundred fifty dollars. Add the credit, and you may come out ahead.
scenes.caption: WHEN IT WORKS

scenes.text: But if you travel once a year, forget to use the credit, and rarely visit lounges, the same card can cost you hundreds of dollars a year for benefits you never touch. A simple no fee card with two percent cash back might leave you better off. The card company is betting you'll be the second person, and many people are.
scenes.caption: WHEN IT DOESN'T

scenes.text: A simple rule. Only pay an annual fee if the benefits you actually used last year, in dollars, clearly beat the fee. And never, ever, pay an annual fee on a card where you carry a balance. At that point, you're paying twice. Once for the card, and once for the interest.
scenes.caption: BENEFITS USED VS FEE

scenes.text: Let me answer the questions people ask me most about credit cards.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: Question one. Should I just cut up all my cards? If cards consistently lead you into debt, using debit or cash for a while can be a smart reset. But if you can pay in full, cards offer real advantages, like stronger fraud protection than many debit cards, and building credit history. The card isn't the enemy. Carrying a balance is.
scenes.caption: CUT THEM UP?

scenes.text: Question two. Can I negotiate my interest rate? Often, yes, especially if you've paid on time for a while. Call, ask politely for a lower APR, and mention competing offers if you have them. It doesn't always work, but it costs a five minute call. Even a few percentage points can save real money on a balance.
scenes.caption: NEGOTIATE YOUR RATE

scenes.text: Question three. Does paying in full hurt my credit because the bank doesn't make money? No. Your credit score is based on things like paying on time and how much of your limit you use, not on how much interest you pay. Paying in full every month is one of the best things you can do for your score.
scenes.caption: DOES PAYING IN FULL HURT?

scenes.text: Question four. When is the best time to pay? At minimum, by the due date. But your balance on the statement closing date is often what's reported to the credit bureaus. If you want a lower reported balance, paying before the statement closes can help. Either way, never pay late.
scenes.caption: WHEN TO PAY

scenes.text: Question five. Are store cards ever worth it? Sometimes, if you shop at that store often and pay in full. But store cards often have higher interest rates and deferred interest promotions. For most people, a general card with simple rewards works better.
scenes.caption: STORE CARDS?

scenes.text: Question seven. Do card companies make money even if I pay in full? Yes, mainly through swipe fees paid by merchants, and sometimes through annual fees. That's why they're still happy to have you. But they make far less from you than from someone who carries a balance, and that's exactly the position you want to be in.
scenes.caption: IF I PAY IN FULL?

scenes.text: And question six. What if I'm already deep in card debt? Start with a small emergency fund so new surprises don't add debt. Stop using the cards for now. List every balance and rate, and choose a payoff method. Call your issuers and ask about lower rates or hardship programs. And if you feel overwhelmed, look for a nonprofit credit counseling agency. Many offer free or low cost help.
scenes.caption: ALREADY IN DEBT?

scenes.text: Before we go, five warning signs that your card is using you, instead of the other way around. One. You don't know your APR. Two. You've paid interest in three or more of the last twelve months. Three. You use one card to pay another, or take cash advances to cover bills.
scenes.caption: WARNING SIGNS 1 TO 3

scenes.text: Four. You pick purchases to earn points or hit a bonus. And five. You feel a little relief when the minimum payment is small. If two or more of these sound familiar, it's time to run the playbook. Start with rule one this month: aim to pay the full statement balance, and if you can't yet, pick a fixed payment that clears it on a date you choose. Then put that date on your calendar and celebrate it when it comes.
scenes.caption: WARNING SIGNS 4 AND 5

scenes.text: Quick recap. Credit card companies make money through interest, swipe fees, late fees, annual fees, balance transfer fees, cash advances, foreign transaction fees and penalty rates. More than one hundred billion dollars in interest alone in a single year.
scenes.caption: THE EIGHT WAYS
scenes.short_hook: 8 ways credit card companies make money from you

scenes.text: They keep it flowing with design: the minimum payment anchor, rewards that make you spend, deferred interest promotions, rising credit limits and painless payments. And you flip the deal with ten rules, starting with the most important one. Pay in full, every month, on autopay.
scenes.caption: FLIP THE DEAL

scenes.text: If you want the full plan, from paying off cards to building real wealth, it's in my playbook. The link is in the description. And if credit card debt is part of a bigger loop, watch my video on why most people stay broke, and how to escape. I'm Ryan Rover. See you in the next one.
scenes.caption: RYAN
